overview:
Kartika Purnima (also called Kartik Poonam or Kartik Poonam) is the full‑moon day of the lunar month of Kartika (October–November). In the broader Indian religious landscape it is associated with river rituals, boat‑floating ceremonies, and various regional observances, but within Jain traditions it has a distinct, tirtha‑centred character.

In Jainism, Kartika Purnima marks the formal reopening of major pilgrimage activity after the four‑month monsoon period known as caturmāsa or caumāsā. During caturmāsa, monks and nuns remain in one place, and laypeople often intensify vows, fasting, scriptural study, and ethical reflection. When Kartika Purnima arrives, the emphasis shifts from monsoon‑season restraint to renewed movement, especially toward celebrated tīrthas (pilgrimage sites). The most prominent of these is Śatruñjaya (Shatrunjay Giriraj) near Palitana in Gujarat, a hill covered with temples and revered across Śvetāmbara and many Digambara communities.

For many Jains, Kartika Purnima is the traditional day on which the large‑scale yātrā (pilgrimage) to Śatruñjaya begins again after the rains. Devotees climb the hill, perform pūjā to the images of the Tīrthaṅkaras, recite the Navakāra (Namokāra) Mantra, and engage in collective worship. The day is considered especially auspicious for accruing puṇya (merit) through darśana (vision of the Jina), dāna (charity), and self‑discipline. In some narrative traditions, Kartika Purnima is also linked to the liberation of exemplary devotees at Śatruñjaya, reinforcing the hill’s status as a kalyāṇaka‑charged site where spiritual progress is intensified.

Dietary and daily‑practice transitions are also associated with Kartika Purnima. In many communities, the strict avoidance of leafy vegetables observed during caturmāsa is relaxed after this day, under guidance from local saṅgha leadership. The shift is framed not as a return to laxity but as a re‑ordering of practice: the monsoon vows have been completed, and now the practitioner re‑enters ordinary routines with renewed awareness of ahiṃsā (non‑violence), aparigraha (non‑possessiveness), and samyag‑caritra (right conduct).

While Kartika Purnima does not correspond to one of the five great kalyāṇakas (womb‑descent, birth, renunciation, omniscience, liberation) of a Tīrthaṅkara, it sits within the ritual year as a hinge between the monsoon retreat and the subsequent cycle of festivals. In Śvetāmbara practice, for example, the nirvāṇa of Mahāvīra is commemorated on the dark‑moon night of Kartika (Diwali), and five days later Jñāna‑pañcamī (the festival of knowledge) is celebrated. Kartika Purnima, falling between these observances, functions as a practical and devotional marker: the lamps lit for Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa and the reverence for scriptural knowledge on Jñāna‑pañcamī are complemented by the embodied act of climbing Śatruñjaya and other tīrthas on the full‑moon night.

Across sectarian lines, the core Jain meaning of Kartika Purnima is remarkably consistent: it is a day of renewed pilgrimage, collective worship, and transition out of caturmāsa discipline. Local customs—such as specific vows, regional hymns, or community feasts—vary, but the underlying orientation remains toward deepening devotion to the Jinas, strengthening ethical resolve, and remembering the liberating potential of contact with sacred places. Modern Jain communities often integrate charitable activities, educational programs, and youth‑focused events into Kartika Purnima observances, extending the traditional emphasis on puṇya into contemporary forms of social responsibility.

primary_sources.title: Śrī Śatruñjaya Māhātmya (Shatrunjaya Mahatmya)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to various Jain authors; composite text
primary_sources.original_text:
कार्तिके पूर्णिमायां तु यः कुर्यात् शत्रुंजये गिरेः ।
दर्शनं जिनदेवानां स पुण्यैः समलंकृतः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
kārtike pūrṇimāyāṃ tu yaḥ kuryāt śatruñjaye gireḥ |
darśanaṃ jinadevānāṃ sa puṇyaiḥ samalaṃkṛtaḥ ||
primary_sources.translation: On Kartika Purnima, whoever undertakes (pilgrimage) to the hill of Śatruñjaya and beholds the Jina‑deities becomes adorned with merits.
primary_sources.notes: This verse represents the kind of praise found in Śatruñjaya Māhātmya literature, which extols the hill’s sanctity and associates specific lunar dates, including Kartika Purnima, with heightened merit. Exact wording varies across manuscripts and editions; the line here is a representative formulation rather than a critical edition. The text belongs to corpus tier B–C (traditional commentary and devotional literature informed by earlier narrative traditions).

primary_sources.title: Kalpa‑sūtra (Śvetāmbara canonical text)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu
primary_sources.original_text: कार्तिकस्य कृष्णपक्षे अमावास्यायां भगवान् महावीरः निर्वाणं प्राप्नोति ।
primary_sources.transliteration: kārtikasya kṛṣṇapakṣe amāvāsyāyāṃ bhagavān mahāvīraḥ nirvāṇaṃ prāpnoti.
primary_sources.translation: In the dark half of Kartika, on the new‑moon night, Lord Mahāvīra attains nirvāṇa.
primary_sources.notes: Although this passage refers to Kartika Amāvasyā (the new‑moon night) rather than Kartika Purnima, it anchors the broader Kartika period in Jain memory as the time of Mahāvīra’s liberation. The proximity of Kartika Purnima to this kalyāṇaka contributes to the month’s ritual density: Diwali (Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa), Kartika Purnima (pilgrimage and transition from caturmāsa), and Jñāna‑pañcamī (festival of knowledge) form a cluster of observances. The Kalpa‑sūtra is a tier A canonical text; the Sanskritized line here reflects a common recensional form of the Prakrit original.

primary_sources.title: Navakāra (Namokāra) Mantra – liturgical usage on Kartika Purnima
primary_sources.author: Anādi (beginningless) mantra; no single human author
primary_sources.original_text:
णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं,
णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं,
णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं ।
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ,
ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ,
ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
Obeisance to the Arihants, obeisance to the Siddhas,
obeisance to the Ācāryas, obeisance to the Upādhyāyas,
obeisance to all Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: The Navakāra Mantra is recited throughout the Jain ritual year and is central to Kartika Purnima observances at Śatruñjaya and other tīrthas. Pilgrims chant it while ascending the hill, performing pūjā, and marking the transition out of caturmāsa. The text itself is tier A (core liturgical formula), while its specific association with Kartika Purnima practice belongs to tier D (community education and ritual manuals).

primary_sources.title: Caturmāsa‑vrata descriptions in later ritual manuals
primary_sources.author: Various Jain ācāryas and ritual compilers
primary_sources.translation: At the completion of the caturmāsa‑vow, on Kartika Purnima, pilgrimage to tīrthas should be undertaken according to scripture.
primary_sources.notes: Ritual handbooks and vrata‑texts from both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions prescribe the timing of vows and pilgrimages. While wording differs by author and region, many explicitly link the end of caturmāsa with Kartika Purnima as the recommended day for tīrthayātrā. These sources are generally tier B–D, reflecting codified practice rather than primary doctrine.

misconceptions.myth: Kartika Purnima is primarily a Hindu river and boat festival and has no particular significance in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Although Kartika Purnima is widely observed in non‑Jain contexts, it holds a distinct place in the Jain ritual year as the traditional restart of major pilgrimage activity—especially to Śatruñjaya—after caturmāsa. Jains use the day for darśana of the Jinas, collective worship, and ethical renewal, grounded in their own tirtha‑focused traditions.

misconceptions.myth: Kartika Purnima is a mandatory fasting day for all Jains, and breaking fast on this date is always considered a serious religious fault.
misconceptions.reality: There is no universally binding rule that Kartika Purnima must be observed through fasting by all Jains. Some individuals or communities may adopt specific vows, but the central emphasis is on pilgrimage, worship, and transition from monsoon disciplines. Decisions about fasting and dietary practice on this day are guided by local saṅgha norms, personal capacity, and, where relevant, medical advice; they are not imposed as an absolute requirement.

misconceptions.myth: Kartika Purnima directly commemorates one of the five great kalyāṇakas of a Tīrthaṅkara, like Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa.
misconceptions.reality: The five kalyāṇakas—womb‑descent, birth, renunciation, omniscience, and liberation—are tied to specific dates and narratives in Jain texts. Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa, for example, is remembered on Kartika Amāvasyā (Diwali), not on Kartika Purnima. Kartika Purnima is important as a practical and devotional marker in the ritual calendar, especially for pilgrimage and post‑caturmāsa transition, but it is not itself a kalyāṇaka date.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain sects observe Kartika Purnima in exactly the same way, with identical rituals and interpretations.
misconceptions.reality: Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, as well as sub‑traditions like Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth, share a broad recognition of Kartika Purnima as an auspicious time for pilgrimage and worship. However, specific practices—such as the details of vows, preferred tīrthas, liturgical sequences, and community programs—vary by region, lineage, and historical development. The underlying orientation toward devotion, ahiṃsā, and ethical renewal is common, but uniformity of ritual is neither expected nor required.
